about.title: Pathways into Complexity
about.lede: Lineages, practices, and methods for working in complex systems, with cases, organizations, and live resources from the Systems Change Learning Guide.
about.intro: We're launching a learning tool about complexity, its history, the thinkers behind it, and new ways for you to start to see complexity in your daily life.
mission: Make the ideas and practices for complex work easy to find, understand and use, for anyone, whatever work they do.
Show where those ideas came from, and the people and traditions who shaped them.
Help you notice complexity in your own work and life, and take a first small step.
about.thanks: We give thanks and acknowledgment to Nora Bateson and others who have lit the path and inspire us to keep walking.
use: Look up an idea, a method or a thinker in plain English.
Find a path into the work you do now, or the work you want to do.
See how ideas connect on the maps, and build your own trail.
Tell us what's wrong or missing, so the guide gets better.

kinds.name: Lineage
kinds.desc: A body of ideas that changes how you understand systems. It informs action without prescribing it.

kinds.name: Practice
kinds.desc: A way of being together that shifts perception and relationship. It works indirectly and breaks when aimed at an output.

kinds.name: Method
kinds.desc: A structured process with steps and artifacts, aimed at a designed outcome. It can be commissioned and reported on.

kinds.name: Structure
kinds.desc: An arrangement of authority, decision-making, and feedback. It changes who decides and how information flows.

kinds.name: Field
kinds.desc: A domain where lineages, practices, methods, and structures meet a context. It is where you work, not how.

kinds.name: Tradition
kinds.desc: A whole way of knowing held by peoples and places. It enters through relationship, consent, and shared power.

kinds.name: Hybrid
kinds.desc: A pathway that is several kinds at once. Watch for the method part being taken and the rest dropped.

orientations.name: Consent before command
orientations.line: Move when no one has a reasoned objection, rather than waiting for everyone to agree or for someone to order it.
orientations.ask: Who has not yet been asked whether they can live with this?

orientations.name: Match the variety
orientations.line: A response has to be as varied as the situation it meets. Do not simplify people to fit the system.
orientations.ask: Where are we forcing many different lives through one channel?

orientations.name: Widen the choices
orientations.line: Act so that the people affected have more options afterward, not fewer.
orientations.source: Heinz von Foerster, the ethical imperative
orientations.ask: Does this close doors for anyone who was not in the room?

orientations.name: Take only what is given
orientations.line: Relationship before extraction. Ask, take what is offered, share it, and give something back.
orientations.source: Robin Wall Kimmerer, the Honorable Harvest
orientations.ask: What are we taking from this community, and what are we returning?

orientations.name: Many contexts, no master frame
orientations.line: Every issue lives in family, work, body, place, and history at once. No single discipline or worldview holds all of it.
orientations.ask: Which context are we ignoring because it does not fit our frame?

orientations.name: Learning over proving
orientations.line: Treat results as information for the next move, and hold people accountable for learning, not for hitting numbers they do not control.
orientations.source: Human Learning Systems, developmental evaluation, Deming
orientations.ask: What did we learn that changes what we do next?

orientations.name: Power in plain sight
orientations.line: Name who decides, whose issues never reach the table, and which beliefs make the arrangement feel natural.
orientations.source: Steven Lukes, John Gaventa, Paulo Freire
orientations.ask: Which form of power is doing the work here without being named?

braids.why: Relational sensing beside a structured change process. The friction shows what each assumes about intention.
Post-humanist inquiry beside practical sensemaking. Both distrust tidy plans for different reasons.
Reciprocity beside commons governance. Two routes to the same insight about shared resources.

braids.pair: Service design + developmental evaluation + transition design
braids.why: Journey, learning loop, and long horizon for government innovation.
Hosting without power analysis can launder existing hierarchies; power analysis without hosting can stay academic.
Regulated bodies make better decisions in the first hours, and recover better afterward.

journeys.title: From crisis response to city innovation
journeys.who: quiet-heron started in government crisis response, working with small, ritual-rich communities, and later moved into a city innovation role inside a reluctant bureaucracy.

stages.where: Starting point: crisis response in small communities
stages.note: What they already know: communities self-organize in a crisis, ritual holds people through disruption, and regulated bodies make better decisions. These pathways name and deepen that knowledge.

Sort ordered from complex problems so procedure can stay procedural. Read resistance as a system defense rather than a personal failing. Learn where procurement, budgets, and audit actually push back.

Host Warm Data Labs alongside the structured methods, not upstream of them, to loosen fixed perception. Use service design and developmental evaluation for accountable, learning-based change. Build a community of practice with the people inside who already work this way.

journeys.braid: Crisis and ritual knowing carried into the institution: the experience of communities adapting fast is proof of what the bureaucracy could do if its constraints loosened.

journeys.title: From corporate innovation to civic partnerships
journeys.who: amber-finch ran an innovation team in a large company and now brokers partnerships between business, city government, and community groups.

stages.note: Comfortable with experiments, portfolios, and customer research. Less practiced at working where no one owns the problem.
Learn why design thinking alone can flatten communities into users, and how power shapes who gets to define the problem.
Convene rather than run. Move money toward trust and portfolios, measure learning instead of outputs, and help partners tell a shared story of why change is needed now.

journeys.braid: Business speed braided with civic patience: portfolio thinking is an asset in public work once it is paired with shared power.

pathways.name: Cybernetics, the shared foundation
pathways.overview: Steering through feedback: how systems regulate themselves, and how observers are part of what they observe.
pathways.road: Norbert Wiener → W. Ross Ashby (requisite variety) → Heinz von Foerster (second-order cybernetics) → Maturana and Varela → Gordon Pask (conversation theory) → Paul Pangaro
pathways.mix: Gregory Bateson and Margaret Mead at the Macy Conferences, Stafford Beer
pathways.policy: Requisite variety as a design test: services must match the variety of people's lives. Beer's Project Cybersyn is the classic, contested case of cybernetic government.
pathways.lens: Complexity as variety. Ashby's law says anything that steers a system must be able to match the variety of what it faces. Later cyberneticians added that the observer is part of the system.
explainer: Cybernetics studies how systems steer themselves using feedback: a thermostat, a body keeping its temperature, a team adjusting after a result. Its founders in the 1940s and 50s saw the same patterns in machines, brains and societies.
A later branch, second-order cybernetics, added that the observer is part of the system being observed, so how you look shapes what you find. Much of the rest of this map grows from these ideas.
practice: Draw one loop you are part of: what you do, what changes, how you find out, what you do next.
Ask where the feedback is slow, missing, or filtered before it reaches the people who decide.
Check requisite variety: list the situations you face, then the responses you have. Where the first list is longer, you will lose control.
Name yourself as an observer. Write down what your position lets you see and what it hides.

sector_notes.biz: Control systems, dashboards and management reporting are cybernetic, whether or not anyone calls them that.
sector_notes.ngo: Programmes that hear from beneficiaries only once a year are steering with a very slow loop.
sector_notes.health: Body regulation (temperature, blood sugar) was a founding example, and clinical audit is a feedback loop on care.
sector_notes.edu: Gordon Pask's conversation theory treats teaching as two systems adjusting to each other.
sector_notes.com: Neighbourhood groups steer well when people see the results of what they did quickly.

key_ideas.defn: When the result of an action loops back and shapes the next action.
Ashby's law: to steer something, your responses need to be at least as varied as the situations you face.
Cybernetics that includes the observer: how you look is part of what you find.
Stafford Beer's model of the five functions any organization needs to survive and adapt.
A system keeping something steady, like body temperature, by correcting drift.

pathways.plain_overview: How systems steer themselves through feedback, and why the observer is part of the picture.
pathways.plain_policy: Designing services that can respond to the real variety of people's lives, instead of forcing everyone through one process.

pathways.name: The formal science of complex systems
pathways.overview: Mathematical and computational study of emergence, networks, adaptation, and self-organization across physics, biology, and society.
pathways.road: Ilya Prigogine (dissipative structures) → Santa Fe Institute → network science (Barabási, Strogatz, Watts) → NECSI (Yaneer Bar-Yam)
pathways.mix: Hermann Haken (†2024, synergetics), Stuart Kauffman
pathways.policy: Agent-based models and network analysis of service systems, epidemics, and markets to test policy before rollout.
pathways.lens: Complexity as many agents following simple local rules, producing emergent, non-linear behaviour that can be modelled but rarely predicted precisely.
explainer: Complexity science studies systems made of many parts that interact, such as cells, ant colonies, cities and markets. The parts follow fairly simple local rules, yet together they produce patterns that none of them planned: traffic jams, epidemics, price bubbles, the shape of a flock.

Researchers use computer models, network maps and mathematics to study how these patterns emerge and when they suddenly shift. The field's main lesson for practice is humility: you can often understand how a complex system behaves without being able to predict exactly what it will do next.
practice: Pick a pattern you care about (waiting lists, rents, school choice) and ask which local rules people follow that add up to it.
Sketch the network: who is connected to whom, and which few nodes hold many connections.
Play with an agent-based model on Complexity Explorer or NetLogo before trusting a forecast.
Look for tipping points: where would a small push cause a big shift?

sector_notes.biz: Supply chains and markets behave like networks; a failure at one hub spreads widely.
sector_notes.ngo: Network maps show which partners hold a coalition together and where it would break.
sector_notes.health: Epidemic models and hospital flow models come straight from this field.
sector_notes.edu: Classrooms show emergence: the mood of a class is not any one pupil's doing.
sector_notes.com: Local patterns like who shops where or who trusts whom are emergent and can shift quickly.

key_ideas.defn: When a whole shows patterns that none of its parts have on their own.
Order that arises from local interactions without anyone in charge.
A computer simulation of many individual agents following rules, to see what patterns emerge.
The study of how things are connected and how connections shape what spreads.
A threshold where a small change flips a system into a different state.

pathways.plain_overview: The science of how many simple parts, each following local rules, produce patterns nobody designed: flocks, traffic, markets, epidemics.
pathways.plain_policy: Used to model epidemics, traffic, and markets, and to warn planners that a system can tip suddenly when it crosses a threshold.

pathways.name: Relational, transcontextual, and post-humanist knowing
pathways.overview: Knowing through relationships rather than parts. Attends to how contexts shape each other and questions the human-centered, modern frame itself.
pathways.road: Gregory Bateson (Steps to an Ecology of Mind) → Nora Bateson (Warm Data, Combining) → Bayo Akomolafe (These Wilds Beyond Our Fences) → Vanessa Machado de Oliveira (Hospicing Modernity)
pathways.mix: Tyson Yunkaporta (Sand Talk), Donna Haraway (Staying with the Trouble), Karen Barad (agential realism), Isabelle Stengers. Joanna Macy (†2025) bridged systems theory, Buddhism, and deep ecology.
pathways.policy: Shows how policy categories fragment lived lives. Warm Data Labs with public teams, and the practice of hospicing institutions that no longer serve.
pathways.lens: Complexity as relationship: nothing exists on its own, and what something is depends on its connections, including its connection to whoever is looking.
explainer: This pathway gathers thinkers who say we understand the world best through relationships, not by breaking it into separate parts. Gregory Bateson traced how mind is spread across organism and environment. Others question the idea that humans stand apart from the rest of life.

It also asks hard questions about modern ways of knowing. Bayo Akomolafe and Vanessa Machado de Oliveira ask how even our efforts to fix things can repeat the patterns that caused harm, and invite slowing down and staying with difficulty rather than rushing to solutions.
practice: Take one problem and describe it from five contexts: family, work, health, money, place.
Notice when you reach for a quick solution, and stay one more conversation with the question.
Ask what the situation looks like from beings or places with no voice in the room.
Read one text slowly with others, and talk about what it did to you, not just what it said.

sector_notes.biz: Shows up in regenerative business and in questioning growth as a default.
sector_notes.ngo: Invites charities to examine how help can repeat the harms it set out to fix.
sector_notes.health: Relational care sees illness through a person's whole web of relationships.
sector_notes.edu: Relational pedagogy treats learning as something that happens between people.
sector_notes.com: Community work that starts from relationships rather than needs assessments.

key_ideas.defn: Bateson's idea that mind is a pattern across organism and environment, not something inside a head.
A problem lives in many contexts at once, and each shapes the others.
Caring for a dying way of life well, so something new can emerge, rather than propping it up.
Questioning the idea that humans stand apart from and above the rest of life.
Karen Barad's view that things come into being through their relationships.

pathways.plain_overview: A family of thinkers who start from relationships rather than separate things, and question the idea that humans stand apart from the world.
pathways.plain_policy: Shows up as a challenge rather than a tool: it asks policy to notice what its categories leave out and who is not in the room, including the land.

pathways.name: Nora Bateson and Warm Data
pathways.overview: Writer, filmmaker, and President of the International Bateson Institute. She carries her father Gregory's ecology of mind into living practice through Warm Data: information about the interrelationships that bind a complex system, found only by moving across contexts.
pathways.road: Gregory Bateson → An Ecology of Mind (film, 2010) → Small Arcs of Larger Circles (2016) → Warm Data Labs and host trainings → Combining (2023). Key ideas: transcontextual inquiry, symmathesy (mutual learning within living systems), aphanipoiesis (unseen coalescence toward vitality).
pathways.mix: Bayo Akomolafe, Tyson Yunkaporta, Otto Scharmer (as a structured counterpoint), the hosting practices
pathways.policy: Warm Data Labs hosted with public staff and residents change how people inside the system perceive and relate to an issue. Whatever policy or design follows comes from that shifted ground in its own time, not from findings harvested and handed over.
pathways.lens: Complexity as interdependence across contexts: a problem lives in many contexts at once, and learning happens between them, in what Bateson calls symmathesy.
explainer: Nora Bateson, daughter of Gregory Bateson, carries his ecology of mind into practice. Her central idea is Warm Data: information about how the parts of a system relate, which you can only find by looking across many contexts at once, such as family, economy, health and culture.

Warm Data Labs are gatherings where people move between small conversations, each framed by a different context, and talk about an issue from their own lives. There is no goal and no output. The aim is that people start to perceive the issue differently, and change follows from that.
practice: Pick an issue and talk about it with a friend through three contexts in turn: family, money, health.
Notice when you want a takeaway, and let the conversation stay open instead.
Attend a Warm Data Lab before trying to host one; host training is offered by the Bateson Institute.
Keep a note of patterns that show up across contexts, not inside one.

sector_notes.biz: Used in leadership retreats to loosen fixed views of a problem.
sector_notes.ngo: Helps community programmes see how one issue tangles with others.
sector_notes.health: Shows how illness is bound up with work, family and place.
sector_notes.edu: Bateson writes on education for a confusing future; labs are run with teachers and students.
sector_notes.com: Labs are often hosted locally, open to anyone in a neighbourhood.

key_ideas.defn: Information about how parts of a system relate, gathered across many contexts at once.
Living things learn and change together, in context. No part learns alone.
A problem lives in many contexts at once: family, economy, health, culture.
Bateson's word for the unseen ways things come together toward vitality.
A gathering where people talk about an issue through many contexts in turn, with no set outcome.

pathways.plain_overview: Nora Bateson's work on how living systems learn together across contexts, and Warm Data Labs: conversations that look at an issue through many parts of life at once.
pathways.plain_policy: Warm Data Labs hosted with public staff and residents shift how people see an issue. Any policy follows from that changed ground in its own time, not from harvested findings.

pathways.name: Indigenous and land-based knowledge
pathways.overview: Knowledge held in relationship with land, kin, and story, where reciprocity and pattern are themselves ways of knowing.
pathways.road: Vine Deloria Jr. → Gregory Cajete (Native Science) → Robin Wall Kimmerer (Braiding Sweetgrass, the Honorable Harvest) → Tyson Yunkaporta (Sand Talk)
pathways.mix: Leroy Little Bear, Winona LaDuke, Elinor Ostrom on the commons
pathways.policy: Indigenous-led stewardship and co-management of land and water, reciprocity as a design principle, and consultation that shares power instead of extracting input.

links.t: Center for Native Peoples and the Environment

pathways.lens: Complexity as kinship and pattern: knowledge lives in relationship with land and community over generations, and right relationship is part of what makes it true.
explainer: Indigenous and land-based knowledge is knowledge held by peoples in long relationship with particular lands, waters and kin. It is carried in story, ceremony, language, practice and law, and it treats reciprocity and responsibility as part of knowing.

This pathway points to Indigenous authors who write for wider audiences, like Robin Wall Kimmerer and Tyson Yunkaporta. It is not a set of techniques to borrow. Engaging well means relationship, consent, credit and shared power, guided by the communities whose knowledge it is.
practice: Learn whose land you are on, and what the nations there ask of visitors and neighbours.
Read Indigenous authors in their own words before reading about them.
When a project draws on Indigenous knowledge, ask who was consulted, who consented, and who benefits.
Support Indigenous-led organizations with money and decision power, not only invitations.

sector_notes.biz: Free, prior and informed consent is a standard for projects on Indigenous land.
sector_notes.ngo: Conservation groups are shifting toward Indigenous-led stewardship.
sector_notes.health: Culturally grounded care, led by Indigenous health services, improves outcomes.
sector_notes.edu: Land-based education and Indigenous science sit alongside Western science in some curricula.
sector_notes.com: Co-management of land and water shares authority between nations and governments.

key_ideas.defn: Taking only what is given, and giving back in return, as a principle of relationship.
Kimmerer's guidelines for taking from the land with respect, so it can keep giving.
Seeing with the strengths of Indigenous and Western knowledge together, from Mi'kmaw Elder Albert Marshall.
The right of Indigenous peoples to agree or refuse before projects affect their lands.
Knowledge that comes from long relationship with a particular place.

pathways.plain_overview: Ways of knowing held by Indigenous peoples and land-based communities, where knowledge comes from long relationship with a place and carries obligations.
pathways.plain_policy: Co-governance of land and water with Indigenous nations, free, prior and informed consent, and recognizing traditional knowledge as evidence on its own terms.

pathways.name: Presencing, Theory U, and Social Presencing Theater
pathways.overview: Change that starts by suspending habitual seeing, sensing the whole, and letting new possibilities take form through the group.
pathways.road: Kurt Lewin (action research) → Argyris and Schön → Peter Senge → Otto Scharmer (Theory U, shaped in part by his interviews with Francisco Varela) → Arawana Hayashi (Social Presencing Theater, sensing a system through embodied movement)
pathways.mix: David Bohm (On Dialogue), Katrin Kaufer, Adam Kahane (transformative scenario planning)
pathways.policy: Co-sensing with residents and frontline staff before anything is designed. u.lab runs are widely used by public teams. Social Presencing Theater is hosted as embodied sensing, not as a technique for gathering input.
pathways.lens: Complexity as the future emerging: the quality of attention in a group shapes what it can bring into being, so change begins with how people see.
explainer: Theory U describes a journey for groups facing change. Instead of jumping from a problem to a solution, a group goes down the U: suspending habitual judgements, sensing the whole system, and connecting at the bottom with what wants to emerge. Then it comes up the other side by prototyping and building.

Otto Scharmer and the Presencing Institute developed it from interviews with many leaders and thinkers. Social Presencing Theater, created by Arawana Hayashi, uses simple movement so groups can sense a system with their bodies. The free u.lab course has reached many public-sector teams.
practice: Before your next project, go on a learning journey to see the system from the other side.
Practise listening at four levels: downloading, factual, empathic and generative.
Try a short stuckness-to-movement exercise from Social Presencing Theater.
Prototype quickly once an idea crystallizes, and learn from real use.

sector_notes.biz: Used in leadership programmes and organizational change.
sector_notes.ngo: Coalitions use u.lab hubs to build shared awareness.
sector_notes.health: Health systems have run Theory U journeys with patients and staff.
sector_notes.edu: u.school applies it to education transformation.
sector_notes.com: Community hubs run u.lab locally.

key_ideas.defn: Sensing and acting from the highest future possibility, from presence plus sensing.
A change process that moves through seeing, sensing and presencing before prototyping.
Listening that only confirms what you already think.
Visiting places and people in a system to see it freshly.
Arawana Hayashi's movement practice for sensing a system with the body.

pathways.plain_overview: Otto Scharmer's Theory U: slow down, sense the whole situation with others, let go of old assumptions, then prototype what wants to emerge.
pathways.plain_policy: Co-sensing with residents and frontline staff before designing anything. u.lab is widely used by public teams. Social Presencing Theater is hosted as embodied sensing, not a way of gathering input.

pathways.name: The metacrisis and meaning
pathways.overview: Treats interlocking ecological, social, and epistemic crises as one pattern rooted in how modern culture perceives and makes meaning.
pathways.road: Bateson and Edgar Morin (†2026) → Iain McGilchrist (The Matter with Things) → Jonathan Rowson (Perspectiva) → Zak Stein and John Vervaeke
pathways.mix: Vanessa Machado de Oliveira, Nora Bateson
pathways.policy: Long-horizon governance, and the sensemaking and meaning-making capacity democracies need to handle intertwined crises.
pathways.lens: Complexity as one pattern beneath many crises: the way a culture attends to the world shapes the problems it produces and the solutions it can see.
explainer: The metacrisis is the idea that climate breakdown, inequality, polarization and other crises are not separate problems but symptoms of a deeper pattern in how modern culture perceives, values and makes sense of the world.

Thinkers here, including Iain McGilchrist, Jonathan Rowson and Zak Stein, look at attention, meaning, education and the health of public sensemaking. Their claim is that technical fixes alone will not be enough without changes in how people see, and that this inner work is also public work.
practice: Pick two crises you care about and ask what they have in common at the level of values and attention.
Notice where your own attention goes in a day, and what that trains you to see.
Join or host a small reading circle on Perspectiva or McGilchrist and discuss what it changes in your work.
Ask what an institution would need to sense the long term, not just the next cycle.

sector_notes.biz: Raises questions about attention-harvesting business models.
sector_notes.ngo: Asks charities whether single-issue campaigns can address shared roots.
sector_notes.health: Links mental health to meaning and the wider culture.
sector_notes.edu: Education for the metacrisis focuses on wisdom and sensemaking, not only skills.
sector_notes.com: Local groups explore meaning and practice together in study circles.

key_ideas.defn: The idea that many crises share one root in how modern culture sees and makes meaning.
Several crises interacting so the whole is worse than the sum.
John Vervaeke's term for the loss of shared ways to make sense of life.
McGilchrist's argument that culture has come to favour a narrow, grasping kind of attention.
Working out together what's going on in an unclear situation, before deciding what to do.

pathways.plain_overview: The idea that today's crises in climate, politics, technology and meaning are linked, with a shared root in how we think and what we value.
pathways.plain_policy: Rarely a policy tool. It shows up as a frame for long-term risk, for questioning growth as the main goal, and for linking inner change to institutional change.

pathways.name: Semiotics: signs, codes, and meaning-making
pathways.overview: How anything comes to mean something: words, images, rules, forms, tracks in the snow. Meaning is not stored in things but made in a three-way relation between a sign, what it points to, and whoever reads it, and whole cultures are woven from these relations.
pathways.road: Charles Sanders Peirce (icon, index, symbol; semiosis) → Ferdinand de Saussure (signifier and signified) → Yuri Lotman (the semiosphere, Tartu–Moscow school) → Umberto Eco (A Theory of Semiotics) → Eduardo Kohn (How Forests Think, semiotics beyond the human)
pathways.mix: Roland Barthes (myth), Thomas Sebeok, Gregory Bateson, the narrative change pathway, biosemiotics
pathways.policy: Public signs, forms, and warnings are sign systems. Semiotics helps check what a message actually signals to different readers, design warnings meant to outlast the people who made them, and see how official categories shape what a system can notice.

pathways.lens: Complexity as meaning-making: what a sign means depends on a three-way relation between the sign, what it points to and whoever reads it, so meaning is always in motion and different for different readers.
explainer: Semiotics is the study of signs: anything that stands for something else to someone. Words, pictures, traffic lights, smoke meaning fire, a uniform meaning authority. Charles Sanders Peirce described three kinds: icons, which resemble what they stand for; indexes, which are connected to it, like a footprint; and symbols, which work by convention, like most words.

From there semiotics looks at how whole cultures run on sign systems. Saussure showed that meaning comes from differences within a system. Yuri Lotman described the semiosphere, the shared space of meaning a culture lives in. Eduardo Kohn extends the question beyond humans: in How Forests Think, he shows how the Amazonian forest is full of other beings interpreting signs.
practice: Take one public form or sign and ask three different people what it tells them; compare.
Sort the signs in a service into icons, indexes and symbols, and check which depend on knowledge some users lack.
When a message must last, use several kinds of sign together and repeat it in more than one channel.
Ask what an official category (like 'household' or 'disability') makes visible and what it hides.

sector_notes.biz: Branding and user interface design are applied semiotics.
sector_notes.ngo: Campaigns test how symbols land with different audiences.
sector_notes.health: Warning labels and patient information depend on signs being read as intended.
sector_notes.edu: Media literacy teaches students to read images and texts as sign systems.
sector_notes.com: Public art and place names carry meanings that differ between communities.

key_ideas.defn: The study of signs: anything that stands for something else to someone.
Peirce's three kinds of sign: by resemblance, by connection, and by convention.
Saussure's split between the form of a sign and the concept it carries.
Lotman's term for the shared space of signs a culture lives in.
The process by which something comes to stand for something else to someone.

pathways.plain_overview: The study of signs: how words, images, symbols and objects come to mean something, and how cultures make some meanings seem natural.
pathways.plain_policy: Public messaging, warning signs and symbols meant to last. The best-known case is marking nuclear waste sites so that people 10,000 years from now stay away.

pathways.name: Living systems and regeneration
pathways.overview: Life as self-producing and interdependent, applied to ecological resilience and regenerative design of cultures and economies.
pathways.road: Maturana and Varela (autopoiesis) → Fritjof Capra → Daniel Christian Wahl (Designing Regenerative Cultures), alongside C.S. Holling → Carl Folke (resilience)
pathways.mix: Donella Meadows, Joanna Macy

pathways.lens: Complexity as life itself: self-making networks that keep renewing themselves and their surroundings.
explainer: Living systems thinking starts from what life does: living things make and remake themselves, depend on each other, and adapt to change. Maturana and Varela called this self-making autopoiesis. Fritjof Capra and others showed how the same principles apply to ecosystems and human communities.

Two practical strands grew from it. Resilience thinking studies how social-ecological systems absorb shocks and reorganize. Regenerative design asks how human activity can leave places healthier than before, not just do less harm.
practice: Treat your place as a living system: map flows of water, food, energy and people.
Ask of any project whether it leaves the place more or less able to renew itself.
Look for slow variables, like soil health or trust, that shape what is possible later.
Design for diversity and redundancy, not just efficiency.

pathways.name: Biosemiotics and the Umwelt
pathways.overview: Life runs on signs, not just chemistry. Every organism lives in its own Umwelt, the world as its senses and needs make it meaningful, and living systems are webs of interpretation from cells to ecosystems.
pathways.road: Jakob von Uexküll (Umwelt, A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans) → Thomas Sebeok (zoosemiotics) → Jesper Hoffmeyer (Signs of Meaning in the Universe, semiotic freedom) → Kalevi Kull (Tartu biosemiotics, ecosemiotics) → Terrence Deacon (Incomplete Nature)
pathways.mix: Gregory Bateson (a difference that makes a difference), Maturana and Varela, Charles Sanders Peirce, Eduardo Kohn, Timo Maran (ecosemiotics)
pathways.policy: Conservation and urban planning that ask what a place means to the species living there, not only how many there are: Umwelt-based analysis of city green spaces, and reintroduction projects that read local human meanings of an animal as carefully as its ecology.

links.t: Ecosemiotics at the University of Tartu

pathways.lens: Complexity as interpretation: living systems are webs of beings reading signs from each other and their surroundings, so to understand a living system you ask what things mean to whom.
explainer: Biosemiotics studies life as a world of signs. A bacterium swims toward sugar because it reads a chemical gradient as a sign of food. A bird hears an alarm call and flees. A cell responds to a hormone. In each case something stands for something else to a living being, and the being acts on it.

The idea goes back to Jakob von Uexküll, who said every animal lives in its own Umwelt: the slice of the world its senses and needs make meaningful. A tick's world has only a few signs in it. Biosemiotics, developed in Copenhagen and Tartu, argues that meaning is part of nature, not something only human minds add.
practice: Pick an animal near you and list what its world is made of: what it notices, what it ignores, what signals danger or food.
When planning a green space, ask what the place means to the species that use it, not only how many there are.
Read Uexküll's short Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans with a group and walk a place through different Umwelten.
In a reintroduction or conservation project, map what the species means to local people as well as what it needs.

sector_notes.biz: Sensory design and animal welfare draw on how other species perceive.
sector_notes.ngo: Conservation groups use Umwelt thinking to reduce human-wildlife conflict.

pathways.name: Sensemaking and acting in uncertainty
pathways.overview: Practical frameworks for telling ordered problems from complex ones and acting through small, safe-to-fail probes.
pathways.road: W. Ross Ashby → Karl Weick (†2026) → Alicia Juarrero → Dave Snowden (Cynefin) → Glenda Eoyang (Human Systems Dynamics)
pathways.mix: Stacey and Shaw's complex responsive processes
pathways.policy: Cynefin in policy and national risk work, safe-to-fail probes instead of big pilots, and distributed citizen narratives as live evidence.
pathways.lens: Complexity as a domain. In Cynefin, a complex situation is one where cause and effect can only be seen in hindsight, so you run small probes, sense what happens and respond, rather than analyse and plan.
explainer: Sensemaking is how people work out what's going on when a situation is unclear, before deciding what to do. This pathway gathers practical tools for it. The best known is Cynefin, which sorts situations by how well cause and effect can be known: clear, complicated, complex or chaotic.

In clear and complicated situations you can analyse and plan. In complex ones, cause and effect only make sense looking back, so you act in small, reversible steps, watch what happens and adjust. Many organizations get into trouble by treating complex problems as if they had a knowable answer.
practice: Before deciding, sort the situation: is the answer known, knowable by experts, only visible in hindsight, or is it chaos?
For complex issues, design three or four small, safe-to-fail probes instead of one big pilot.
Agree in advance what you would amplify and what would make you stop each probe.
Collect short stories from people affected and look for patterns across many of them, not one star example.

sector_notes.biz: Used to separate operational problems with best practice from market shifts that need probing.
sector_notes.ngo: Helps programmes stop reporting complex work as if it followed a logic model.
sector_notes.health: Clinical protocols suit clear cases; patients with many conditions often sit in the complex domain.
sector_notes.edu: School leaders use it to tell timetable problems apart from culture problems.
sector_notes.com: Neighbourhood groups can run small experiments and keep what works.

key_ideas.defn: A framework from Dave Snowden that sorts situations into clear, complicated, complex and chaotic. Each needs a different way of acting.
Working out together what's going on in an unclear situation, before deciding what to do.
A small experiment designed so that if it fails, the damage is small and you still learn.
In complex situations, act a little, see what happens, then adjust.
Early, faint signs of change that are easy to dismiss.

pathways.plain_overview: Tools for working out what's going on when nobody can know the answer in advance, and acting in small steps.
pathways.plain_policy: Used in government to plan for risk, run small tests instead of big pilots, and treat people's own stories as up-to-date evidence.

pathways.name: Governance and self-organizing structures
pathways.overview: Designing decision structures that use feedback, consent, and distributed authority instead of command and control.
pathways.road: Ashby → Stafford Beer (Viable System Model) → Kees Boeke and Gerard Endenburg (†2025, sociocracy) → Elinor Ostrom (polycentric governance)
pathways.mix: Frederic Laloux, the Buurtzorg case, Indy Johar (Dark Matter Labs)
pathways.policy: Ostrom's design principles for co-governance of shared resources, polycentric arrangements across agencies, and consent-based structures inside teams.
pathways.lens: Complexity as distributed control: no single centre can know enough, so authority and feedback are designed to sit close to the work, linked so the whole can still adapt.
explainer: This pathway is about how groups can govern themselves without a single boss making every call. It gathers tested designs: sociocracy, where decisions are made by consent in linked circles; the Viable System Model, which shows the functions any organization needs; and Elinor Ostrom's principles for communities that manage shared resources like water or forests.

Self-organizing does not mean structureless. These designs are often more explicit than a hierarchy about who decides what, how objections are heard, and how information travels. They spread authority to where the knowledge is.
practice: Map who actually decides what today, including the informal decisions.
Try consent for one recurring decision: proceed unless someone has a reasoned objection that it would cause harm.
Write down the domain of one team: what it can decide without asking.
If you share a resource, check it against Ostrom's eight principles, such as clear boundaries and local monitoring.

sector_notes.biz: Buurtzorg and Haier show self-managing teams at scale; many firms use consent in leadership teams.
sector_notes.ngo: Small charities and co-ops use sociocracy to share decisions with staff and members.
sector_notes.health: Self-managing nurse teams in home care are the best-known example.
sector_notes.edu: Student councils and staff circles can run on consent rather than majority vote.
sector_notes.com: Community land trusts, housing co-ops and allotments are classic commons.

key_ideas.defn: A way of governing with consent decisions in linked circles, so every voice has a route.

A shared resource managed by the community that uses it.

Stafford Beer's model of the five functions any organization needs to survive and adapt.

pathways.name: Emergence in movements and social change
pathways.overview: How small, relational, adaptive actions scale into systemic change without central control.
pathways.road: Grace Lee Boggs and Octavia Butler → adrienne maree brown (Emergent Strategy) → Margaret Wheatley and the Berkana Two Loops model
pathways.mix: Nora Bateson on change that happens between contexts
pathways.policy: Governments hosting rather than directing: funding networks, backing community-led pilots, and using the Two Loops model to steward transitions.
pathways.lens: Complexity as emergence: patterns at scale grow from small, repeated relationships and practices, so how you work locally is the strategy.
explainer: This pathway is about how social change grows from small relationships and practices rather than from a master plan. adrienne maree brown's Emergent Strategy draws on Octavia Butler and Grace Lee Boggs: change spreads like patterns in nature, through many small, adaptive actions.

Margaret Wheatley and the Berkana Institute's Two Loops model describes how, as an old system declines, people build the new one in networks that connect, grow into communities of practice and finally become the new norm. How you work locally is the strategy.
practice: Pick one small practice you want to see in the world and make it how your group works now.
Map the people pioneering the new and connect two of them who have not met.
Name who is hospicing the old system and how you can support them too.
Review your group's work by asking what grew, not just what was achieved.

The idea that how we work at small scale repeats at large scale.
Connections between people who share an interest, the first stage of emergence.
A group that shares a practice and learns from each other over time.

pathways.name: Hosting and participatory practice
pathways.overview: Methods for convening groups so that collective intelligence and new patterns can emerge from the room.
pathways.road: Harrison Owen (Open Space) → Juanita Brown and David Isaacs (World Café) → Art of Hosting (Toke Møller, Chris Corrigan) → Liberating Structures (Lipmanowicz and McCandless) → Warm Data Labs
pathways.mix: David Bohm (On Dialogue), sociocracy, Social Presencing Theater
pathways.policy: Participatory processes, citizens' assemblies, and deliberative forums, with Art of Hosting methods long used in public institutions.
pathways.lens: Complexity in the room: when the right people meet around a real question, the group can produce ideas and commitments no one brought with them.
explainer: Hosting is the craft of convening groups so that they can think and act well together. It brings a family of methods: Open Space, where participants set the agenda; World Café, small rotating table conversations; Circle; and Liberating Structures, 33 simple patterns that replace the usual meeting formats.

The Art of Hosting community teaches these as a practice, not a toolkit. The host's job is to set a clear purpose, invite the right people and create conditions for the conversation that matters, then trust the group.
practice: Write a powerful question for your next meeting, one people actually want to talk about.
Replace one presentation with a 1-2-4-All from Liberating Structures.
Try Open Space for an issue with many owners: let participants set the agenda.
Close with a harvest: decide how the group's thinking will be captured and used.

sector_notes.ngo: Art of Hosting is common in networks and coalitions.

Small table conversations that rotate, so ideas cross-pollinate across a large group.

Capturing what a gathering produced so it can be used.
A question that invites real thinking and matters to the people in the room.

pathways.name: Bohm Dialogue
pathways.overview: Groups suspending assumptions and attending to collective thought as it moves, with no agenda or decision to reach.
pathways.road: David Bohm (On Dialogue) → William Isaacs (Dialogue and the Art of Thinking Together) → Peter Senge's learning organization work
pathways.mix: Otto Scharmer, Nora Bateson, the hosting practices
pathways.policy: Dialogue held for its own sake in cross-agency and community settings, with no decision on the table. Over time it loosens the assumptions that would otherwise harden into policy.

reading.title: The art of dialogue (MIT, on William Isaacs's Dialogue Project)

pathways.lens: Complexity as collective thought: meaning flows through a group and shapes what it can see, so change begins by attending to how the group thinks.
explainer: Bohm Dialogue is a way for a group to think together. People sit in a circle, often for a long time, with no agenda and no decision to make. The aim is to notice how thought moves in the group, and to suspend your assumptions: hold them up to look at, rather than defend them or drop them.

The physicist David Bohm developed it late in life because he saw that collective thought is full of hidden assumptions that cause conflict. William Isaacs and the MIT Dialogue Project brought it into organizations, and Peter Senge made it part of the learning organization.
practice: Gather 10 to 30 people for at least an hour with no agenda except to talk and listen.
When you feel a strong reaction, say what it is rather than arguing from it.
Practise suspension: notice an assumption, say it aloud, and look at it together.
Meet regularly; the practice deepens over several sessions.

sector_notes.biz: Used to rebuild trust between union and management and in leadership teams.

pathways.name: T-groups and sensitivity training
pathways.overview: Small unstructured groups learning from their own here-and-now interaction. The root of much of organization development.
pathways.road: Kurt Lewin → NTL Institute at Bethel, Maine (1947) → Chris Argyris and Edgar Schein (†2023) → Stanford's Interpersonal Dynamics course
pathways.mix: Group Relations, action research
pathways.policy: Leadership development that builds capacity to notice group dynamics, power, and feedback inside public teams.
pathways.lens: Complexity in the here and now: a group's behaviour emerges from its members' interactions, and you learn it best by studying it as it happens.
explainer: A T-group (training group) is a small group that meets with no agenda except to learn from what happens between its members, here and now. People give and receive feedback on how they come across and notice how the group forms, struggles and works.

It began in 1946 when Kurt Lewin's team found that participants learned most when they joined staff discussions of their own behaviour. The National Training Laboratories followed in 1947. T-groups shaped organization development and live on in courses like Stanford's Interpersonal Dynamics, known as Touchy Feely.
practice: Join a structured T-group lab with trained facilitators; do not improvise one on colleagues.
Practise giving feedback about specific behaviour and its effect on you, not about character.
In meetings, notice who speaks, who is interrupted and what is avoided.
Ask for feedback on one habit and try a small change.

sector_notes.ngo: Builds the self-awareness facilitators need.
sector_notes.health: Group-based learning for clinicians handling difficult relationships.
sector_notes.edu: Interpersonal Dynamics at Stanford and similar courses.

key_ideas.defn: Paying attention to what is happening in the group right now, not to outside topics.
Telling someone the effect their behaviour had on you, specifically and kindly.
Kurt Lewin's term for the forces that shape how groups behave.
A small training group that learns from its own interaction.
Learning by experimenting with behaviour in a safe, temporary setting.

pathways.name: Group Relations
pathways.overview: Temporary learning institutions where members study authority, role, and unconscious group dynamics as they happen.
pathways.road: Wilfred Bion (Experiences in Groups) → A.K. Rice and the Tavistock Institute's Leicester Conference (since 1957) → the A.K. Rice Institute in the US
pathways.mix: T-groups, systems psychodynamics
pathways.policy: Understanding authority and role in bureaucracies, and why systems unconsciously resist the change they commission.
pathways.lens: Complexity below the surface: groups carry unconscious patterns of anxiety and defence that shape what an organization can do.
explainer: Group Relations studies how groups and organizations behave below the surface: the anxieties, fantasies and unspoken assumptions that shape how people take up authority and roles. It grew from Wilfred Bion's work with groups and the Tavistock Institute.

Its main method is the conference, a temporary organization where members study authority and leadership as they happen. The Leicester Conference has run since 1957. The insight for practice: organizations often resist the very change they commission, for reasons nobody says out loud.
practice: Attend a Group Relations conference before applying the ideas to others.
Ask what anxiety a structure or procedure might be protecting people from.
Notice when a group seems to be acting on an unspoken assumption, such as waiting for a leader to save it.
Separate the person from the role: what is being asked of the role?

pathways.name: Appreciative Inquiry
pathways.overview: Change that starts from what already gives life to a system rather than from its problems.
pathways.road: David Cooperrider and Suresh Srivastva (Case Western, 1980s) → the 4-D cycle → Appreciative Inquiry Summits for whole-system change
pathways.mix: Positive deviance, World Café
pathways.policy: Whole-system summits with residents, staff, and partners that design from existing strengths.
pathways.lens: Complexity as the stories a system tells about itself: the questions people ask shape what they notice and so what grows.
explainer: Appreciative Inquiry starts change from what already works. Instead of diagnosing problems, people interview each other about high points and strengths, then build a picture of the future from them.

David Cooperrider and Suresh Srivastva developed it in the 1980s at Case Western Reserve University. It usually follows a 4-D cycle: discover, dream, design and destiny (or deliver). Summits bring a whole system into one room, sometimes hundreds of people.
practice: Pair people up to interview each other about a time the organization was at its best.
Pull out the themes that made those moments possible.
Write provocative propositions: bold statements of the future built from those themes.
Ask who is missing from the room, and invite them for the next round.

pathways.name: Work That Reconnects
pathways.overview: A group practice that moves through gratitude, honoring pain for the world, seeing with new eyes, and going forth.
pathways.road: Joanna Macy (†2025) → Molly Young Brown and facilitators worldwide → the Work That Reconnects Network
pathways.mix: Deep ecology, the relational pathway
pathways.policy: Sustaining public servants and communities working on climate and loss, where despair blocks action.
pathways.lens: Complexity as interconnection felt in the body: our pain for the world shows we are part of a larger living system, and acknowledging it frees the energy to act.
explainer: The Work That Reconnects is a set of group practices created by Joanna Macy and colleagues. It moves through a spiral of four stages: coming from gratitude, honouring our pain for the world, seeing with new eyes, and going forth.

It began in the early 1980s as despair and empowerment work, for people overwhelmed by the threat of nuclear war. The core insight is that grief and fear for the world, shared openly, are signs of connection, and can become the energy for action. Macy died in 2025; the Work That Reconnects Network carries the practice on.
practice: Begin a gathering with what people are grateful for.
Make room for people to say what they fear or grieve about the world, without rushing to fix it.
Try a deep-time exercise: imagine speaking with people living 200 years from now.
Close with each person naming one step they will take.

sector_notes.ngo: Sustains activists and climate workers against burnout.
sector_notes.health: Complements care for eco-anxiety and grief.
sector_notes.edu: Used in climate education to help students act from feeling, not despair.
sector_notes.com: Community groups host workshops after local disasters or losses.

Hope as something you do, not something you have.
Imagining across many generations to widen your sense of the present.
Macy's name for the shift from an industrial growth society to a life-sustaining one.
The view that all living things have value in themselves, not only for human use.

pathways.name: Somatic and embodied practice
pathways.overview: Change that lives in the body: how bodies hold history, shape what we can perceive under stress, and settle enough to act together. Treats embodiment as a condition for working in complexity, not a wellness add-on.
pathways.road: Wilhelm Reich and body-oriented psychology → Richard Strozzi-Heckler (somatic leadership) → Staci K. Haines (generative somatics, The Politics of Trauma) → Resmaa Menakem (My Grandmother's Hands, cultural somatics)
pathways.mix: Arawana Hayashi (Social Presencing Theater), Joanna Macy, the crisis and transition cluster
pathways.policy: Trauma-informed services and workplaces, frontline staff regulation in high-stress roles, and noticing how bodies in a room shape what a public meeting can actually hear.

pathways.lens: Complexity lived in the body: history and stress shape what people can perceive, so the capacity to work with complexity depends on bodies that can settle.
explainer: Somatic practice treats the body as where change happens. Under stress, bodies narrow what people can perceive and react from old patterns. Practices that build awareness of breath, posture and sensation help people settle and act with more choice.

Social justice somatics, developed by Staci Haines and generative somatics, links personal trauma to social conditions. Resmaa Menakem's cultural somatics looks at how racialized trauma lives in bodies across generations. For complex work, a settled body is a condition for listening and acting together.
practice: Before a hard conversation, take a minute to feel your feet and lengthen your breath.
Notice where in your body you feel pressure in a meeting, and what you do next.
Practise a centring exercise daily for a month, from Strozzi or generative somatics.
In a group, pause and ask how people are, physically, before deciding.

Bringing attention back to the body to act from choice rather than reaction.

How experience and history live in the body and shape action.

pathways.name: Power analysis
pathways.overview: Making power visible: who decides, whose issues never reach the table, and which beliefs make an arrangement feel natural. The missing question in much systems work.
pathways.road: Steven Lukes (Power: A Radical View, three faces of power) → John Gaventa (Power Cube: spaces, places, and forms of power) → Lisa VeneKlasen and Valerie Miller (A New Weave of Power, JASS)
pathways.mix: Paulo Freire, Michel Foucault, Sasha Costanza-Chock, Group Relations
pathways.policy: Mapping who actually shapes a policy, which consultations are closed, invited, or claimed spaces, and where invisible power (norms, beliefs) keeps residents out.
pathways.lens: Complexity as layered power: visible decisions, hidden agenda-setting, and invisible norms, operating at different levels and in different spaces.
explainer: Power analysis makes power visible. Steven Lukes described three faces of power: who wins in open decisions, who controls which issues ever reach the table, and how beliefs and norms make some arrangements seem natural.

John Gaventa's Power Cube adds spaces (closed, invited, claimed), levels (local to global) and forms (visible, hidden, invisible). Lisa VeneKlasen and Valerie Miller turned these into practical tools for organizers. Much systems work skips power; this pathway puts it back.
practice: Map a decision you care about: who decides, who sets the agenda, and which beliefs keep others out.
Sort the spaces where your issue is discussed into closed, invited and claimed.
Name your own position: where do you hold power, and where do you lack it?
Ask who benefits from things staying as they are.

sector_notes.biz: Stakeholder mapping often misses hidden and invisible power.
sector_notes.ngo: Advocacy groups use the Power Cube to plan campaigns.
sector_notes.health: Shows who shapes health policy and whose voices are missing.
sector_notes.edu: Popular education uses power analysis with learners.
sector_notes.com: Organizers map power before choosing targets.

key_ideas.defn: Lukes' visible, hidden and invisible power: decisions, agenda-setting and shaping beliefs.
Gaventa's tool for analysing the spaces, levels and forms of power.
A space that people create for themselves, outside official channels.
Power that works through norms and beliefs, so people do not see it as power.
Where you stand in relation to power, and how that shapes what you see.

pathways.plain_overview: Tools for seeing power: who decides, whose issues never reach the table, and which beliefs make an arrangement feel natural.
pathways.plain_policy: Mapping who shapes a policy, which spaces are closed, invited or claimed, and where hidden norms keep people out.

pathways.name: Narrative change
pathways.overview: Shifting the deep stories a society uses to make sense of an issue, so different policies become thinkable. Works over years through many voices, not one campaign.
pathways.road: George Lakoff (framing) → FrameWorks Institute (strategic frame analysis) → Narrative Initiative (Toward New Gravity) → Marshall Ganz (public narrative: story of self, us, and now)
pathways.mix: adrienne maree brown, Bayo Akomolafe, Hilary Cottam
pathways.policy: Reframing public problems so structural causes become visible, and giving public servants and residents a way to tell a shared story of why change is needed now.

links.t: FrameWorks Institute: Five questions about framing

pathways.lens: Complexity as shared stories: what a society believes is possible emerges from many stories interacting, and shifting them takes many voices over years.
explainer: Narrative change works on the deep stories a society uses to make sense of an issue. If people believe poverty is about individual choices, policies that address structural causes will seem strange. Change the story, and different policies become thinkable.

George Lakoff showed how frames shape reasoning. The FrameWorks Institute tests which frames help the public understand complex issues. Narrative Initiative focuses on long-term shifts carried by many voices. Marshall Ganz's public narrative helps individuals tell a story of self, us and now that moves people to act.
practice: Write down the story people usually tell about your issue, and who it blames.
Test two framings with people outside your sector and listen to how they respond.
Tell a public narrative: your story of self, the story of us, and the story of now.
Coordinate with others so many voices carry the same deeper story.

sector_notes.biz: Brands shape cultural narratives, for better and worse.
sector_notes.ngo: FrameWorks research guides how charities talk about their issues.
sector_notes.health: Reframing ageing and mental health has shifted public understanding.
sector_notes.edu: Media literacy helps students see frames at work.
sector_notes.com: Community storytelling builds shared identity and agency.

key_ideas.defn: How an issue is presented, which shapes how people reason about it.
A widely held, often unspoken story people use to make sense of the world.
Ganz's method: story of self, story of us, story of now.
The ability to shape which stories are told and believed.
A shared mental shortcut people use to understand an issue.

pathways.plain_overview: Changing the deep stories a society uses to make sense of an issue, so different choices become thinkable.
pathways.plain_policy: Telling the story of a public problem so its real causes are visible, and giving staff and residents a shared story of why change is needed now.

pathways.name: Conflict transformation
pathways.overview: Treating conflict as information about a system and a doorway into changed relationships, rather than a problem to settle quickly. Holds justice and relationship together.
pathways.road: John Paul Lederach (The Moral Imagination) → Arnold and Amy Mindell (Deep Democracy, Worldwork) → Howard Zehr (restorative justice) → Marshall Rosenberg (Nonviolent Communication)
pathways.mix: Group Relations, T-groups, the somatic pathway, adrienne maree brown
pathways.policy: Restorative approaches in justice, schools, and housing; community mediation; and hosting charged public meetings so minority voices are not steamrolled by consensus.
pathways.lens: Complexity as conflict carrying information: tensions show where a system's relationships and structures are out of step, and working through them can change the whole.
explainer: Conflict transformation sees conflict as a sign that relationships and structures need to change, not just a problem to settle. John Paul Lederach argued that lasting peace needs moral imagination: seeing ourselves in a web of relationships that includes our enemies.

The pathway brings together restorative justice (Howard Zehr), which focuses on repairing harm; Deep Democracy and Worldwork (Arnold and Amy Mindell), which bring minority voices into the room; and Nonviolent Communication (Marshall Rosenberg), which helps people hear the needs behind positions.
practice: Before mediating, ask what relationships need to change, not only what deal is possible.
In a restorative circle, ask: what happened, who was affected, and what is needed to repair it?
Listen for the need behind a position and say it back.
In a group decision, ask whether any minority view has not been heard yet.

sector_notes.biz: Workplace mediation and restorative approaches to grievances.
sector_notes.ngo: Peacebuilding organizations work at community and national scale.
sector_notes.health: Restorative approaches after clinical harm support patients and staff.
sector_notes.edu: Restorative practice in schools reduces exclusions.
sector_notes.com: Community mediation and circles address neighbour disputes.

key_ideas.defn: Lederach's capacity to see a web of relationships that includes adversaries.
Responding to harm by repairing it, with those affected involved.
The Mindells' practice of bringing all voices, including marginal ones, into awareness.
Rosenberg's method of naming observations, feelings, needs and requests.
Working with conflict to change relationships and structures, not just to settle it.

pathways.plain_overview: Treating conflict as information about a system and a chance to change relationships, not just a problem to settle.
pathways.plain_policy: Restorative approaches in courts, schools and housing, community mediation, and public meetings run so minority voices are heard.

pathways.name: Crisis, disaster, and high reliability
pathways.overview: What people and organizations do when normal order breaks. Disasters tend to produce mutual aid, not panic, and the best-run high-risk organizations stay alert to small failures instead of trusting their plans.
pathways.road: Enrico Quarantelli (disaster sociology) → Karl Weick and Kathleen Sutcliffe (Managing the Unexpected, high reliability organizing) → Rebecca Solnit (A Paradise Built in Hell) → Daniel Aldrich (social capital in recovery) → Dean Spade (mutual aid)
pathways.mix: Cynefin's chaotic domain, the somatic pathway, Ostrom on self-organized commons
pathways.policy: Emergency management that works with spontaneous volunteers rather than against them, investing in neighborhood ties before disasters, and after-action learning without blame.

links.t: Weick and Sutcliffe: high reliability principles

pathways.lens: Complexity as the unexpected: high-reliability organizations stay alert to small failures and defer to whoever has the most relevant expertise in the moment.
explainer: This pathway draws on research into what really happens when disaster strikes. Contrary to the image of panic, people usually help each other: Rebecca Solnit calls the communities that form a paradise built in hell. Daniel Aldrich showed that social ties predict recovery better than money.

High reliability organizations, like aircraft carriers and nuclear plants, stay safe by staying alert to small failures and letting the person with the most relevant knowledge decide. Mutual aid, which Dean Spade describes, is how communities organize to meet needs directly.
practice: Map who knows whom on your street before an emergency, and who might need help.
Run a short after-action review after any incident: what happened, why, and what we will change.
Practise deferring to expertise: in a crisis, who in the room knows most about this?
Plan to work with spontaneous volunteers rather than turning them away.

sector_notes.biz: High reliability practices in aviation, energy and manufacturing.
sector_notes.ngo: Humanitarian groups increasingly back local mutual aid.
sector_notes.health: Hospitals adopt high reliability principles to reduce harm.
sector_notes.edu: Schools plan for emergencies with community ties in mind.
sector_notes.com: Mutual aid networks formed widely during the COVID-19 pandemic.

key_ideas.defn: An organization that operates safely in high-risk conditions by staying alert to small failures.
People meeting each other's needs directly, as equals, outside formal charity.
The networks and trust that let people act together.
Treating small errors as signs of bigger risks.
Letting whoever knows most about the situation make the call.

pathways.plain_overview: What people and organizations do when normal order breaks, and how high-risk organizations stay alert to small failures.
pathways.plain_policy: Emergency planning that works with volunteers, builds neighbourhood ties before disasters, and learns afterwards without blame.
