pathways.name: Ritual, liminality, and transition
pathways.overview: Why ritual matters when systems change. Transitions pass through a threshold where old roles dissolve before new ones form, and communities have long held people through that in-between.
pathways.road: Arnold van Gennep (rites of passage) → Victor Turner (liminality, communitas) → William Bridges (endings, neutral zone, new beginnings) → Francis Weller (grief as communal work)
pathways.mix: Work That Reconnects, Bayo Akomolafe, Vanessa Machado de Oliveira (hospicing), Indigenous and land-based knowledge
pathways.policy: Marking endings when programs close or teams merge, grief and memorial work after a crisis, and treating reorganizations as transitions people move through, not org charts.

links.t: William Bridges Associates: What is transition?
Francis Weller: The Geography of Sorrow (The Sun)

pathways.lens: Complexity as threshold: systems change passes through an unstable in-between time, and how people are held there shapes what emerges.
explainer: Every real transition passes through an in-between time, when old roles have ended and new ones have not formed. Arnold van Gennep described rites of passage in three phases: separation, the threshold, and return. Victor Turner called the threshold liminality, and the bond people form there communitas.

William Bridges applied this to organizations: change is the external event, but transition is the inner process of letting go, the neutral zone, and new beginnings. Francis Weller writes about grief as communal work. Systems change involves endings, and ritual helps people through them.
practice: When something ends, mark it: name what is being lost and thank it.
Tell people in a reorganization that a confusing middle period is normal.
Hold a simple ritual for a team ending or a programme closing.
Make space for grief in community after a loss.

sector_notes.biz: Bridges' transition model is used in change management.
sector_notes.ngo: Charities closing programmes use endings rituals with staff and partners.
sector_notes.health: Hospice and bereavement care hold people through the most personal transitions.
sector_notes.edu: Graduations and orientation are rites of passage that can be designed with care.
sector_notes.com: Grief rituals and memorials help communities after disasters.

key_ideas.defn: The in-between state of a transition, when old roles are gone and new ones have not formed.
A ritual marking a transition, with separation, threshold and return.
The strong bond among people going through a threshold together.
Bridges' term for the confusing middle of a transition.
Grieving together as a community, as Weller describes.

pathways.plain_overview: Why ritual matters in change: transitions pass through a threshold where old roles end before new ones begin, and communities have long held people through that in-between.
pathways.plain_policy: Marking endings when programmes close or teams merge, and helping people through reorganizations instead of just redrawing the chart.

pathways.name: Public policy and government innovation
pathways.overview: Moving public management from targets and linear delivery toward learning, relationships, experimentation, and adaptive stewardship.
pathways.road: Rittel and Webber (wicked problems) → Donella Meadows (leverage points) → Geoff Mulgan (collective intelligence, public imagination) → Toby Lowe (Human Learning Systems) → Hilary Cottam (Radical Help, the relational state)
pathways.mix: Mariana Mazzucato (mission-oriented policy), Christian Bason (design for policy), Indy Johar (Dark Matter Labs), Bill Sharpe (Three Horizons), UNDP's portfolio approach to systems change
pathways.policy: This is the home field for the policy lens. Read it alongside the Strategy, money, and accountability cluster, where budgets, contracts, and metrics decide whether any of this survives contact with a real institution.

links.t: UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose
OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation

pathways.lens: Complexity as wicked problems: issues with no final definition, no single owner, and no solution that stays solved, so policy has to keep learning.
explainer: This pathway asks how government can work when the problems it faces are tangled and changing. Instead of setting targets and rolling out a fixed plan, it treats public services as systems that need to learn: trying things, listening to people, building relationships and adjusting.

It brings together ideas like wicked problems, leverage points and mission-oriented policy, and practical movements like Human Learning Systems and the relational state. The common thread is that outcomes come from many actors working together, so the state's job is often to steward the system rather than control it.
practice: Pick one service and ask who else shapes the outcome it is measured on.
Replace one target with a learning question that staff and residents review together every few months.
Spend a day with frontline staff before writing the next policy paper.
Fund a small portfolio of approaches rather than one pilot, and agree how you will learn across them.

sector_notes.biz: Firms that deliver public contracts feel this most: payment by results versus alliance contracts.
sector_notes.ngo: Charities are often the frontline of public services and can push for learning-based commissioning.
sector_notes.health: Integrated care systems are attempts to run health and care as one learning system.
sector_notes.edu: Education policy that sets curriculum but trusts schools to adapt sits in this space.
sector_notes.com: Community groups are partners, not just consultees, in the relational state.

key_ideas.defn: A problem with no clear definition, no right answer, and no point where it is solved for good.
A place in a system where a small shift produces big change, from Donella Meadows.
An approach to public management built on learning, relationships and system stewardship instead of targets.
Policy organized around a bold, concrete goal that many sectors work toward.
Looking after the health of a whole system rather than controlling its parts.

pathways.plain_overview: How governments are learning to work on problems that do not stay solved, through public innovation, missions and learning-based management.
pathways.plain_policy: The home field for government work. Read it with the money and accountability pathways, where budgets, contracts and targets decide what survives.

pathways.name: Systemic design and futures
pathways.overview: Design practice scaled up to whole systems, paired with ways of using the future to act differently in the present.
pathways.road: Horst Rittel → Birger Sevaldson (gigamapping) → Hugh Dubberly and Paul Pangaro → Riel Miller (futures literacy) → Bill Sharpe (Three Horizons)
pathways.mix: Dan Hill (Dark Matter and Trojan Horses), Christian Bason, Dunne and Raby (critical design), Stuart Candy (experiential futures)
pathways.policy: Government policy labs, anticipatory governance, futures literacy for civil servants, and portfolio approaches instead of single-bet programs.
pathways.lens: Complexity as a mess to be seen whole: map the system richly enough that people can find leverage, and use several futures to loosen today's assumptions.
explainer: Systemic design takes the tools of design, like drawing, prototyping and working with users, and applies them to whole systems such as food, mobility or care. Designers make big visual maps, sometimes called gigamaps, so a group can see a whole system at once and find where to act.

Futures work is its companion. Methods like Three Horizons, scenarios and futures literacy help people imagine several possible futures and use them to make better choices today, instead of betting on one forecast.
practice: Make a big shared map of a system with the people in it, on one wall, before choosing an intervention.
Run a Three Horizons conversation: what is fading, what is emerging, what is the bridge between them?
Write two or three short scenarios and test your plan against each.
Look for the pockets of the future already present today.

sector_notes.biz: Strategy teams use scenarios and horizon scanning to stress-test plans.
sector_notes.ngo: System maps help coalitions agree where each organization fits.
sector_notes.health: Gigamaps of patient pathways show where handoffs fail.
sector_notes.edu: Futures literacy is taught in schools and universities through UNESCO labs.
sector_notes.com: Community futures workshops let residents imagine their place in 30 years.

key_ideas.defn: Making very large, detailed visual maps of a system so a group can see it whole.
A framework that looks at the fading present, the emerging future, and the transition between them.
The skill of using imagined futures to understand and act in the present.
A coherent story of a possible future, used to test plans, not to predict.
Systematic thinking about possible futures to inform decisions now.

pathways.plain_overview: Design for whole systems and long time horizons: mapping big messes, imagining several futures, and finding where to intervene.
pathways.plain_policy: Futures and foresight units in government, systemic design labs, and Three Horizons conversations before long-term policy commitments.

pathways.name: Complexity economics and new economic models
pathways.overview: The economy as an evolving, adaptive system of people and institutions rather than an equilibrium machine.
pathways.road: Herbert Simon (bounded rationality) → W. Brian Arthur (increasing returns) → Eric Beinhocker (The Origin of Wealth) → Kate Raworth (Doughnut Economics)
pathways.mix: J. Doyne Farmer (Making Sense of Chaos), Elinor Ostrom, Mariana Mazzucato
pathways.policy: City Doughnut portraits (Amsterdam adopted the model in 2020), mission-oriented innovation, and regulation that expects adaptation.
pathways.lens: Complexity as an economy that is always forming: agents adapt to patterns they create together, so markets rarely settle into equilibrium.
explainer: Mainstream economics often pictures the economy as a machine that settles into balance. Complexity economics sees it instead as an ecosystem that never stops changing: people and firms learn, copy each other and invent, so the economy keeps creating new patterns, booms and crashes.

New economic models build on this. Kate Raworth's Doughnut asks how to meet everyone's needs without overshooting the planet's limits. Others look at wellbeing economies and post-growth. Together they argue that the goal of an economy is a choice, and that it should be set openly.
practice: Draw your city or organization's Doughnut: which social needs fall short, which planetary limits are overshot?
Ask where increasing returns lock in a winner, and whether that is healthy.
Swap one growth metric for a wellbeing indicator and see what changes in the conversation.
Look at who benefits from a policy over time, not only at launch.

sector_notes.biz: Platform markets show increasing returns: the leader gets stronger simply by being ahead.
sector_notes.ngo: Wellbeing economy alliances bring charities into economic policy.
sector_notes.health: Health is a big part of any wellbeing economy and of the social foundation in the Doughnut.
sector_notes.edu: Rethinking Economics and CORE teach economics with these ideas built in.
sector_notes.com: Local Doughnut groups and community wealth building apply it at neighbourhood scale.

key_ideas.defn: When being ahead makes it easier to get further ahead, so small early leads lock in.
Kate Raworth's model: meet everyone's needs without overshooting the planet's limits.
Herbert Simon's idea that people decide with limited time, information and attention.
A state of balance. Complexity economics argues real economies rarely settle into one.
An economy designed to deliver human and ecological wellbeing rather than growth for its own sake.

pathways.plain_overview: Economics that treats the economy as a complex, changing system inside society and nature, rather than a machine that settles at equilibrium.
pathways.plain_policy: Doughnut-based city strategies, wellbeing budgets, and modelling that expects instability rather than equilibrium.

pathways.name: Strategy under uncertainty
pathways.overview: Strategy that assumes the future cannot be predicted: rehearse several futures, map how value chains evolve, and build options that benefit from surprise.
pathways.road: Pierre Wack (Shell scenarios) → Adam Kahane (transformative scenario planning) → Simon Wardley (Wardley Mapping) → Nassim Nicholas Taleb (antifragility)
pathways.mix: Three Horizons, Cynefin, futures literacy
pathways.policy: Scenario work before long-lived infrastructure or budget commitments, and mapping which public capabilities are commodity versus genuinely new before procuring them.

links.t: Pierre Wack: Scenarios, Uncharted Waters Ahead (HBR)
Adam Kahane: Transformative Scenario Planning (SSIR excerpt)

pathways.lens: Complexity as an open future: plans must hold up across several possible worlds, and strategy is a way of noticing and responding, not a fixed route.
explainer: Strategy under uncertainty starts from an honest admission: nobody can predict the future well enough to plan around a single forecast. Instead, it uses tools that prepare an organization for several futures at once.

Scenarios rehearse plausible futures so leaders notice early signs. Wardley Maps show how the parts of a business or service evolve from new to commodity, so you know what to build and what to buy. Antifragility asks how to design things that gain from shocks rather than break.
practice: Write two to four scenarios with people who disagree, then ask what you would do in each.
Draw a Wardley Map of one service: what users need, and how evolved each component is.
List decisions that are hard to reverse and slow them down; speed up the easy-to-reverse ones.
Name the early signs that would tell you which scenario is unfolding, and watch for them.

sector_notes.biz: Shell's scenarios are the classic case; Wardley Mapping is widely used in tech strategy.
sector_notes.ngo: Scenarios help charities plan when funding and policy may shift sharply.
sector_notes.health: Pandemic preparedness is scenario work; the plans that held up were the flexible ones.
sector_notes.edu: Universities use scenarios to think about demographics and technology.
sector_notes.com: Transformative scenario planning brought opposing groups together in South Africa.

key_ideas.defn: Rehearsing several plausible futures to make better decisions now.
A map of a value chain showing how each component evolves from novel to commodity.
Nassim Taleb's word for things that get stronger from shocks and stress.
Keeping choices open so you can act when the future becomes clearer.
Adam Kahane's method where opponents build scenarios together to change the situation, not just adapt to it.

pathways.plain_overview: Strategy for a future you cannot predict: rehearse several futures, map how things are changing, and keep options open.
pathways.plain_policy: Scenario work before long-lived infrastructure or budget commitments, and Wardley maps before procurement.

pathways.name: Funding and budgeting for adaptation
pathways.overview: Money that can follow learning. Replaces fixed annual budgets and single big bets with rolling allocation, portfolios of experiments, and funders who trust grantees.
pathways.road: Jeremy Hope and Robin Fraser (Beyond Budgeting) → Bjarte Bogsnes (Equinor) → UNDP portfolio approach → Trust-Based Philanthropy Project
pathways.mix: Human Learning Systems, developmental evaluation, Mariana Mazzucato
pathways.policy: Multi-year flexible funding, portfolio budgets for missions, and grant terms that let providers change course when they learn something.

links.t: Bogsnes: Beyond Budgeting at Equinor (Drucker Forum)
UNDP: portfolio approach to system transformation

pathways.lens: Complexity as money that has to adapt: when outcomes are uncertain, funding works best in portfolios and rolling cycles that can follow what is learned.
explainer: Most money in organizations and government is tied to fixed annual budgets and detailed plans. That makes it hard to change course when you learn something. This pathway collects ways to let money follow learning instead.

Beyond Budgeting replaces the annual budget with rolling forecasts and decisions made closer to the work. Portfolio approaches fund several experiments at once and move money toward what works. Trust-based philanthropy gives grantees flexible, multi-year money and lighter reporting.
practice: Find one budget line that could move from annual to rolling review.
Fund three small, different approaches to one problem instead of one big bet.
Ask a grantee what reporting they would drop if they could, and drop it.
Agree up front how money will move when you learn something, so changing course is not a failure.

sector_notes.biz: Handelsbanken and Equinor run without traditional annual budgets.
sector_notes.ngo: Unrestricted, multi-year grants let charities adapt; trust-based funders lead this.
sector_notes.health: Pooled budgets across health and care follow patients instead of departments.
sector_notes.edu: Schools with flexible budgets can respond to what pupils need mid-year.
sector_notes.com: Participatory grant-making lets residents decide where community money goes.

key_ideas.defn: Running an organization without fixed annual budgets, using rolling forecasts and devolved decisions.
Funding several linked experiments together and managing them as a whole.
Grant-making built on flexible money, light reporting and shared power with grantees.
A forecast updated regularly instead of fixed once a year.
Money a grantee can spend on whatever the work needs.

pathways.plain_overview: Money that can follow learning: rolling budgets, portfolios of experiments, and funders who trust the people they fund.
pathways.plain_policy: Multi-year flexible funding, portfolio budgets for missions, and grant terms that let providers change course when they learn something.

pathways.name: Measurement and accountability
pathways.overview: Why targets distort what they measure, and what accountability can look like when outcomes are emergent. Moves from proving results to learning in public.
pathways.road: Donald Campbell and Charles Goodhart (the laws named after them) → Mark Moore (public value, the strategic triangle) → Jerry Muller (The Tyranny of Metrics) → Toby Lowe (accountability for learning)
pathways.mix: Deming, developmental evaluation, Human Learning Systems
pathways.policy: Replacing target regimes with learning reviews, reporting what changed and why, and holding services accountable for the health of relationships and systems, not activity counts.

links.t: Jerry Muller: The Tyranny of Metrics (Chronicle)
Moore's strategic triangle (Atlas of Public Management)

pathways.lens: Complexity as outcomes nobody controls alone: numbers can inform learning, but used as targets in a complex system they distort the work they are meant to measure.
explainer: When a number becomes a target, people start working to the number instead of the purpose behind it. This pathway explains why that happens and what to do instead. Campbell's and Goodhart's laws describe the distortion; Jerry Muller's The Tyranny of Metrics collects the evidence.

The alternative is not to stop measuring but to measure for learning. Public value thinking asks what a service is for and who it answers to. Accountability for learning holds people to account for reflecting honestly and improving, not for hitting numbers they do not control.
practice: List your targets and ask, for each one, how someone could hit it while making things worse.
Turn one target into a question you review together: what did we learn, and what will we try next?
Collect a few stories alongside the numbers so you can see what the numbers miss.
Ask who the measures are for: the people served, the staff, or the funder.

sector_notes.biz: Sales targets that encourage mis-selling are a classic case of Goodhart's law.
sector_notes.ngo: Funders and charities can agree learning questions instead of output counts.
sector_notes.health: Waiting-time targets have led to gaming, such as patients held in ambulances.
sector_notes.edu: Test-score targets narrow teaching to the test.
sector_notes.com: Community groups can track what matters to members, not just attendance.

key_ideas.defn: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
The more a number is used for decisions, the more it gets corrupted and corrupts the work.
Mark Moore's idea that public managers should create value the public cares about, with legitimacy and capacity to deliver it.
Holding people to account for learning and improving, not for numbers they do not control.
Hitting a target in ways that defeat its purpose.

pathways.plain_overview: Why targets distort what they measure, and how to be accountable when outcomes are emergent.
pathways.plain_policy: Swapping targets for learning reviews: report what changed and why, and judge services on the health of relationships, not activity counts.

pathways.name: Government plumbing
pathways.overview: The rules, contracts, and routines where reluctant bureaucracies actually push back. Procurement, delivery, regulation, and frontline discretion decide whether complexity methods survive.
pathways.road: Michael Lipsky (Street-Level Bureaucracy) → Charles Sabel and Jonathan Zeitlin (experimentalist governance) → relational commissioning (Plymouth Alliance) → Jennifer Pahlka (Recoding America)
pathways.mix: Nesta on anticipatory regulation and sandboxes, Hilary Cottam, service design
pathways.policy: Alliance contracts instead of payment by results, policy written with delivery teams at the table, regulatory sandboxes, and trusting frontline discretion instead of scripting it away.
pathways.lens: Complexity in the machinery: rules, contracts and routines interact in ways no one designed, and they quietly decide which new ideas survive.
explainer: New ideas about complexity often die in the ordinary machinery of government: procurement rules, contracts, budgets, audits, and job descriptions. This pathway is about that machinery, which some people call the plumbing.

Michael Lipsky showed that frontline workers make policy every day through the choices they make. Experimentalist governance sets broad goals and lets local units find their way, reviewing together. Jennifer Pahlka's Recoding America shows how layers of rules make simple services fail. The lesson: if you want change to last, change the plumbing.
practice: Trace one simple request through every rule and form it touches, and count the steps.
Ask procurement to sit in on the design of a service, not just the tender.
Try an alliance contract where providers share one outcome instead of competing.
Ask frontline staff which rule they work around most, and why.

sector_notes.biz: Suppliers to government live with this plumbing and can help redesign contracts.
sector_notes.ngo: Charities feel the effects of short contracts and payment by results.
sector_notes.health: Commissioning rules decide whether health and care can work as one.
sector_notes.edu: Funding formulas and inspection regimes shape what schools can try.
sector_notes.com: Grant rules and licensing decide whether community groups can act quickly.

key_ideas.defn: Michael Lipsky's insight that frontline workers effectively make policy through daily choices.
Set broad goals centrally, let local units try ways to meet them, and review together.
Buying services through ongoing relationships and shared goals rather than fixed specifications.
One contract where several providers share responsibility for an outcome.
A safe space where new approaches can be tested under relaxed rules with close watching.

pathways.plain_overview: The rules, contracts and routines where bureaucracies actually resist change: procurement, regulation, budgets and frontline discretion.
pathways.plain_policy: Contracts based on partnership instead of payment by results, policy written with the people who deliver it, and trust in frontline judgement.

pathways.name: Teams and learning cultures
pathways.overview: The team-level conditions that let people surface bad news, learn fast, and organize around flow instead of hierarchy.
pathways.road: Amy Edmondson (psychological safety, teaming) → Jeff Gothelf and Josh Seiden (Sense and Respond) → Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais (Team Topologies)
pathways.mix: Deming, sociocracy, T-groups
pathways.policy: Blameless reviews in public agencies, product teams that own a service end to end, and outcomes over outputs in digital delivery.

links.t: Amy Edmondson: Building a psychologically safe workplace (TEDx)

pathways.lens: Complexity in the team: learning depends on people speaking up and on how teams connect, so the structure of conversations matters as much as the structure of tasks.
explainer: Most complex work happens in teams. This pathway is about the conditions that let a team learn: people feel safe to raise problems and admit mistakes, the team is organized around the flow of work, and it measures success by outcomes for users rather than tasks finished.

Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety showed that the best hospital teams reported more errors, because they talked about them. Team Topologies offers a few simple team types and ways they interact. Sense and Respond applies these ideas to whole organizations.
practice: Start a meeting by inviting the problem nobody has raised yet, and thank whoever raises it.
Run a blameless review of something that went wrong: what happened, what made sense at the time, what will change.
Ask the team what outcome for users it is trying to change this quarter.
Map how your team depends on others and cut one handoff.

sector_notes.biz: Common in tech and product teams; Google's Project Aristotle highlighted psychological safety.
sector_notes.ngo: Small teams under pressure benefit from blameless reviews and clear outcomes.
sector_notes.health: Edmondson's research began in hospital teams; speaking up saves lives.
sector_notes.edu: Teaching teams that share failures openly improve faster.
sector_notes.com: Volunteer groups need the same safety to raise problems early.

key_ideas.defn: A shared belief that the team is safe for speaking up, asking questions and admitting mistakes.
Looking at what went wrong to learn, without seeking someone to punish.
A small set of team types and ways of interacting, to organize around the flow of work.
Judging work by the change it makes for people, not by how much was produced.
Edmondson's word for forming and working in teams on the fly.

pathways.plain_overview: The team habits that let people raise bad news, learn fast, and organize around the flow of work instead of hierarchy.
pathways.plain_policy: Blameless reviews in public agencies, product teams that own a service end to end, and outcomes over outputs in digital delivery.

pathways.name: Corporate innovation and renewal
pathways.overview: How established organizations explore new value while running the current business, and when they need to break apart into smaller self-managing units.
pathways.road: Clayton Christensen (disruptive innovation) → Charles O'Reilly and Michael Tushman (ambidextrous organization) → Henry Chesbrough (open innovation) → Haier (RenDanHeYi microenterprises)
pathways.mix: Buurtzorg, Beyond Budgeting, Wardley Mapping
pathways.policy: Public agencies face the same exploit and explore tension: protected space for new services without starving the ones residents rely on today.
pathways.lens: Complexity as constant renewal: an organization is a living system that must keep exploring while exploiting what works, or its environment will move on without it.
explainer: Established organizations are good at running what they already do and bad at inventing what comes next. This pathway collects research on why, and on how some have managed both.

Disruptive innovation explains how newcomers win by starting where incumbents are not looking. Ambidextrous organizations protect new units from the old ones while sharing what helps. Open innovation looks outside for ideas. Haier's microenterprises go furthest, breaking a giant firm into thousands of small self-managing businesses.
practice: Split your work into run and explore, and protect a small budget for exploring.
Ask where a cheaper, simpler competitor could start today, and talk to those customers.
Invite one outside partner to solve a problem you have kept internal.
Try a small unit with its own customers and its own profit and loss.

sector_notes.biz: This is home ground: Christensen, O'Reilly and Tushman, Chesbrough and Haier.
sector_notes.ngo: Large charities face the same tension between their core programmes and new approaches.
sector_notes.health: Health systems need protected space for new models of care alongside the old.
sector_notes.edu: Universities set up separate units for online learning to avoid being smothered.
sector_notes.com: Community groups can spin off new projects without risking the core.

key_ideas.defn: When a simpler, cheaper offer starts at the bottom of a market and moves up until it displaces leaders.
Running the current business well while exploring new ones.
Using ideas and partners from outside the organization.
Haier's model of thousands of small, self-managing units close to customers.
The tension between using what works and searching for what might work.

pathways.plain_overview: How established organizations explore new value while running the current business, and when they need to break into smaller self-managing units.
pathways.plain_policy: Agencies, like companies, need protected space to try new services without starving the ones people rely on today.

pathways.name: Collaboration across boundaries
pathways.overview: How many organizations work on one shared problem without one of them owning it. The field has moved from shared measurement toward equity and community power.
pathways.road: John Kania and Mark Kramer (collective impact, 2011) → Mark Cabaj and Liz Weaver (Collective Impact 3.0) → Collective Impact Forum's equity turn
pathways.mix: Ostrom, network weaving, Two Loops, Human Learning Systems
pathways.policy: Cross-agency place-based partnerships, shared learning agendas instead of shared KPIs, and residents holding real seats in governance.
pathways.lens: Complexity as shared problems: no single actor can solve them, so progress comes from aligning many actors around learning, with the most affected people holding real power.
explainer: Big social problems are not owned by any one organization. This pathway is about how many organizations, public, private and community, can work on one shared problem together.

Collective impact (2011) set out five conditions, including a common agenda and a backbone organization. Practice since then has moved on: Collective Impact 3.0 shifts from management to movement building, and the field now puts equity and community power at the centre.
practice: Map who already works on the problem and invite the people most affected into the first meeting.
Agree a few shared learning questions before agreeing shared indicators.
Fund a small backbone team whose job is to connect, not to control.
Check who holds decision power in the partnership and whether residents have real seats.

sector_notes.biz: Firms join place-based partnerships as employers, funders and suppliers.
sector_notes.ngo: Charities often host the backbone function.
sector_notes.health: Health partnerships with councils and charities tackle causes of ill health.
sector_notes.edu: Strive in Cincinnati linked schools, colleges and services around children's progress.
sector_notes.com: Community organizations bring legitimacy and knowledge the institutions lack.

key_ideas.defn: Many organizations working on one problem with a common agenda and a backbone team.
A small team that supports a partnership by connecting, convening and keeping data.
A shared understanding of the problem and the change being sought.
Deliberately building connections between people so a network can act.
Residents holding real decision-making power, not only a voice.

pathways.plain_overview: How many organizations work together on one shared problem when no single one owns it.
pathways.plain_policy: Agencies working together in one place, with shared learning instead of shared targets, and residents with real seats at the table.

pathways.name: Design thinking
pathways.overview: Framing problems through empathy, prototyping, and iteration. Strong for bounded problems, weaker where no single solution exists.
pathways.road: Herbert Simon (The Sciences of the Artificial) → Horst Rittel → Nigel Cross (Designerly Ways of Knowing) → Donald Schön (reflection-in-action) → IDEO and the Stanford d.school
pathways.mix: Natasha Iskander's critique of design thinking
pathways.policy: Human-centered problem framing in agency innovation teams. Most useful when paired with complexity methods for problems without one right answer.
pathways.lens: Complexity met by making: you understand a problem better by building rough versions and watching what people do with them.
explainer: Design thinking is a way of solving problems that starts with people. Teams observe and interview users, frame the problem, generate ideas, build quick prototypes and test them, going round the loop several times.

It was popularized by IDEO and the Stanford d.school, building on design research by Herbert Simon, Horst Rittel and Nigel Cross. It works well for bounded problems. Critics, like Natasha Iskander, note that it can keep power with designers and miss systemic causes.
practice: Watch three people use the thing you want to improve, without helping.
Write the problem as a question starting with 'How might we'.
Build a rough prototype in an afternoon and test it the next day.
Ask who is not in the design process who should be.

sector_notes.biz: Product and service development in many firms.
sector_notes.ngo: Human-centred design for programmes, as with the Embrace infant warmer.
sector_notes.health: Patient-centred redesign of clinics and devices.
sector_notes.edu: Design thinking courses at d.schools worldwide.
sector_notes.com: Community makers and civic tech groups prototype local fixes.

key_ideas.defn: Design that starts from the needs and behaviour of the people who will use it.
A rough version of an idea, made to learn quickly.
A question format that turns a problem into an invitation to ideas.
In design thinking, understanding users by watching and listening closely.
Repeating the build-test-learn cycle to improve.

pathways.plain_overview: A human-centred way of solving problems: understand people's needs, generate ideas, and test rough prototypes quickly.
pathways.plain_policy: Used in government to understand residents' needs before designing, and to test ideas cheaply before committing money.

pathways.name: Service design
pathways.overview: Services as journeys across touchpoints, with frontstage experience and backstage systems designed together.
pathways.road: Lynn Shostack (service blueprinting) → Birgit Mager (Köln) → Marc Stickdorn (This Is Service Design Doing) → Lou Downe (Good Services)
pathways.mix: UK Government Digital Service, US Digital Service, 18F (closed 2025)
pathways.policy: End-to-end benefit and permit journeys, service standards, and blueprints that expose the policy and system constraints behind a bad experience.
pathways.lens: Complexity in the journey: a service is many systems meeting one person, and the experience emerges from how front and back stages connect.
explainer: Service design looks at a service the way the person using it experiences it: as one journey from first need to final outcome, across websites, letters, phone calls, counters and waiting rooms. It then designs the frontstage (what people see) and the backstage (the staff, systems and rules behind it) together.

Lynn Shostack introduced the service blueprint in 1984. The UK's Government Digital Service made it central to public services, and Lou Downe set out plain principles for good services. Done well, it exposes the policy and system problems hiding behind a bad experience.
practice: Follow one person through a whole service, from first need to final outcome, and draw it.
Make a service blueprint showing what users see and the backstage work behind each step.
Test a service against Lou Downe's 15 principles of good services.
Fix one handoff where users have to repeat themselves.

sector_notes.biz: Banking, retail and telecoms use service design to cut friction.
sector_notes.ngo: Charities redesign advice and support services around users.
sector_notes.health: Patient journeys through hospitals and GP surgeries.
sector_notes.edu: Student services and admissions redesigned end to end.
sector_notes.com: Community services, such as food banks, mapped from the user's side.

key_ideas.defn: Designing a service end to end: what people experience and the behind-the-scenes work that makes it happen.
A diagram of a service showing what users see, and the backstage work behind each step.
A picture of the steps someone goes through to get something done, and how each step feels.
Lou Downe's plain-language standards for what makes a service work well for the people using it.
Learning directly from the people who use a service: watching, asking, testing.

pathways.plain_overview: Designing a service end to end: what people experience at each step and the behind-the-scenes work that makes it happen.
pathways.plain_policy: Government digital services built around user needs, service standards, and blueprints that join the front line to the back office.

pathways.name: Participatory design and design justice
pathways.overview: Designing with people rather than for them, with power named and shared in the process.
pathways.road: Scandinavian participatory design (Pelle Ehn, Kristen Nygaard) → Elizabeth Sanders (co-design) → Ezio Manzini (Design, When Everybody Designs) → Sasha Costanza-Chock (Design Justice) → Arturo Escobar (Designs for the Pluriverse)
pathways.mix: The relational and Indigenous pathways
pathways.policy: Co-designing programs with the residents they serve, with explicit attention to who holds decision power.
pathways.lens: Complexity as many worlds: the people living with a problem hold knowledge designers lack, and good design shares power with them.
explainer: Participatory design means designing with people, not for them. It began in Scandinavia in the 1970s, when trade unions and designers worked together on new workplace technology so workers had a say.

Co-design (Elizabeth Sanders) and design for social innovation (Ezio Manzini) carried it forward. Design justice (Sasha Costanza-Chock) asks who benefits and who is harmed by design, and centres the people most affected. Arturo Escobar's Designs for the Pluriverse argues for many ways of living, not one.
practice: Invite people affected by a problem to help frame it before any ideas are generated.
Pay participants for their time and expertise.
Share decision power: agree which decisions participants make, not just advise on.
Ask who could be harmed by the design and include them.

sector_notes.ngo: Design justice shapes programmes with communities.
sector_notes.health: Co-production of services with patients and carers.
sector_notes.edu: Co-designing learning spaces with students.
sector_notes.com: Communities design their own spaces and services.

key_ideas.defn: Designing together with the people who will use or be affected by the result.
Design led by marginalized communities, aiming to dismantle structural inequality.
A world where many worlds fit, in Escobar's phrase from the Zapatistas.
Design in which users take part in decisions, rooted in Scandinavian workplace democracy.
Public services designed and delivered with the people who use them.

pathways.plain_overview: Design with, not for: the people affected by a design take part in making it, and design is used to shift power toward communities.
pathways.plain_policy: Co-design with residents as decision-makers, not only informants, and design justice principles in public services.

pathways.name: Transition design
pathways.overview: Design for long-horizon societal transitions, grounded in living systems theory. The design path most explicitly built on complexity.
pathways.road: Terry Irwin, Gideon Kossoff, and Cameron Tonkinwise (Carnegie Mellon)
pathways.mix: Three Horizons, Capra, Meadows
pathways.policy: Long-horizon transitions in energy, food, and care that span agencies and election cycles.
pathways.lens: Complexity as long transition: societies change over decades through many linked shifts, so design must work across scales and timescales at once.
explainer: Transition design is design for long-term societal change, such as moving to sustainable food, energy or transport systems. It was developed at Carnegie Mellon by Terry Irwin, Gideon Kossoff, Cameron Tonkinwise and colleagues.

It asks designers to map the wicked problem and its history, envision a long-horizon future, and design interventions at many levels and timescales that move the system toward it. It draws on living systems and social change theory.
practice: Map your problem's history: how did it come to be this way?
Write a vision for 40 years ahead and work back to now.
Design a small intervention today that points toward that future.
Link projects at household, community and policy scale.

sector_notes.biz: Firms in energy and food use it to plan long transitions.
sector_notes.ngo: Environmental groups apply it to systemic campaigns.
sector_notes.health: Long-term shifts toward prevention and community health.
sector_notes.edu: Taught in design schools as an alternative to short-term projects.
sector_notes.com: Transition Towns and local food networks share the spirit.

key_ideas.defn: Design for long-term societal transitions toward sustainable futures.
A problem with no clear definition, no right answer, and no point where it is solved for good.
Imagining a desired future and working backward to see what steps lead there.
A model of transitions as interactions between niches, regimes and landscapes.
Thinking in decades, not quarters.

pathways.name: Strategic design and policy labs
pathways.overview: Using design to reshape institutions and the rules, budgets, and culture underneath them.

pathways.mix: Geoff Mulgan, Nesta

pathways.lens: Complexity in the institution: services sit on top of rules, money and culture, so lasting change means redesigning that dark matter too.
explainer: Strategic design uses design to change institutions: the rules, budgets, contracts and culture that shape what services can be. Policy labs inside or alongside government test new approaches with civil servants and citizens.

Helsinki Design Lab and Denmark's MindLab were early examples; Policy Lab UK and France's La 27e Région followed. Dark Matter Labs works on the deep infrastructure of finance, ownership and governance. The aim is change that lasts because the system underneath it has changed.
practice: Pick a policy problem and prototype the experience of the policy before writing it.
Work with the people who write budgets and contracts, not just service teams.
Run a small lab with frontline staff and residents for six weeks.
Document what you learn about the institution, not just the product.

Using design to change institutions and the conditions around services.
Dan Hill's term for the hidden rules, culture and money that shape what institutions can do.

Looking after the health of a whole system rather than controlling its parts.

pathways.name: Improvement and adaptive management
pathways.overview: Learning cycles built into daily operations, treating the organization as a system to be continually improved.
pathways.road: W. Edwards Deming (System of Profound Knowledge) → Toyota and Lean → Don Berwick and IHI (PDSA cycles) → Agile
pathways.mix: Plexus Institute's healthcare work, Brenda Zimmerman
pathways.policy: PDSA cycles in public health and service delivery, and continuous improvement units inside agencies.
pathways.lens: Complexity as variation: outcomes come from systems, not individuals, so improvement means learning how the system behaves through many small tests.
explainer: Improvement treats an organization as a system to be improved continually through small cycles of learning. W. Edwards Deming taught that most problems come from the system, not the people, and that leaders must understand variation and learn through Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles.

Toyota and Lean built this into daily work. In health care, Don Berwick and the Institute for Healthcare Improvement spread PDSA cycles widely. Agile software development shares the idea: deliver small, learn, adjust.
practice: Pick one measure and plot it over time on a run chart before reacting to any single result.
Run a PDSA cycle: plan a small change, try it, study the result, act on what you learned.
Ask the people doing the work what gets in their way.
Stop blaming individuals for problems the system produces.

sector_notes.ngo: Quality improvement in programme delivery.
sector_notes.health: IHI and the 100,000 Lives Campaign.
sector_notes.edu: Improvement science in schools through networked improvement communities.
sector_notes.com: Small tests of change in community projects.

key_ideas.defn: Plan-Do-Study-Act: a small cycle of testing a change and learning from it.
Deming's four parts: systems, variation, knowledge and psychology.
The natural ups and downs in any measure; telling noise from signal.
A way of working that removes waste and improves flow.
A graph of a measure over time, to see real change.

pathways.name: Developmental evaluation
pathways.overview: Evaluation built for innovation in complex settings, feeding real-time learning instead of judging afterward.
pathways.road: Michael Quinn Patton → Mark Cabaj and the Tamarack Institute
pathways.mix: Human Learning Systems, Cynefin
pathways.policy: Funding and accountability for adaptive programs, where evaluators help programs learn while they run.
pathways.lens: Complexity as emergent results: when goals and paths are still forming, evaluation must learn alongside the work, not judge it afterward.
explainer: Developmental evaluation supports innovation in complex settings. Instead of judging a programme at the end, the evaluator works alongside the team, feeding back what is happening so the programme can adapt.

Michael Quinn Patton developed it for situations where the goal and the path are still emerging. Mark Cabaj and the Tamarack Institute spread it in community change work. It asks: what are we learning, and what should we do next?
practice: Bring an evaluator into the team from the start, not at the end.
Agree a few learning questions and review them every month or two.
Track what changed in the strategy and why.
Report to funders what was learned, including what did not work.

sector_notes.ngo: Community change initiatives use it to adapt as they go.
sector_notes.health: Evaluating new models of care while they are still forming.
sector_notes.edu: Evaluating school reform while it unfolds.
sector_notes.com: Community-led projects use it to learn together.

key_ideas.defn: Evaluation that supports a programme to adapt while it runs.
A question a team agrees to explore together over time.
A strategy that takes shape through action and learning.
Patton's principle that evaluation should be useful to its intended users.
Evaluation that judges results at the end, which developmental evaluation is not.

pathways.plain_policy: Evaluating innovative programmes and policy experiments where outcomes are emergent and the model is still changing.

pathways.name: Action research
pathways.overview: Inquiry and change as one act, led with and by the people affected.
pathways.road: Kurt Lewin → Paulo Freire and Orlando Fals-Borda (participatory action research) → Peter Reason and Hilary Bradbury
pathways.mix: Chris Argyris (action science), the hosting pathway
pathways.policy: Community-led inquiry into local problems, with residents as co-researchers and co-owners of findings.

links.t: Action Research Network of the Americas

pathways.lens: Complexity known from inside: the people in a situation understand it best by changing it and reflecting together.
explainer: Action research combines research and change into one process. People affected by a problem study it together, act, look at what happened, and act again. Kurt Lewin coined the term in the 1940s.

Paulo Freire and Orlando Fals-Borda developed participatory action research with communities in Latin America, treating them as researchers of their own lives. Peter Reason and Hilary Bradbury brought the many traditions together. Knowledge and power are shared.
practice: Gather people affected by a problem and agree a shared question.
Plan a small action, take it, and meet to reflect on what happened.
Repeat the cycle several times, writing down what you learn.
Share findings back with the community first, in a form they can use.

sector_notes.biz: Action learning and action science in organizations.
sector_notes.ngo: Participatory research with communities served.
sector_notes.health: Patient-led research and participatory health research.
sector_notes.edu: Teacher action research in classrooms.
sector_notes.com: Communities research their own housing, health and environment.

key_ideas.defn: Research and change as one cycle, done with the people affected.
Action research led by communities, linking knowledge to power.
Research where participants are researchers too.
Plan, act, observe, reflect, and repeat.
Action and reflection together, in Freire's sense.

pathways.plain_overview: Research done with people, not on them: participants study their own situation and act on what they learn, in cycles.
pathways.plain_policy: Participatory research with residents to shape policy, and practitioner research inside public services.

pathways.name: Positive deviance
pathways.overview: Finding the uncommon practices that already work inside a community and helping them spread.
pathways.road: Jerry and Monique Sternin
pathways.mix: Plexus Institute, which championed it in healthcare
pathways.policy: Scaling what already works in the field, from frontline caseworkers to communities, before importing outside solutions.
pathways.lens: Complexity as local solutions already present: the answer to a complex problem often exists in the system, practised by a few, waiting to be noticed.
explainer: Positive deviance starts from a simple observation: in almost every community, a few people facing the same problem do better than others, with no extra resources. Finding out what they do differently, and helping it spread, is often faster than importing outside solutions.

Jerry and Monique Sternin developed it with Save the Children in Vietnam in the 1990s, where some poor families had well-nourished children. The method has since been used in health care, education and business.
practice: Define the problem with the community, then find those who succeed against the odds.
Learn what they do differently by watching, not just asking.
Let the community design ways to practise those behaviours, rather than telling them.
Track progress with the community.

sector_notes.ngo: Nutrition and health programmes in many countries.
sector_notes.health: Hospital infection control, through the Plexus Institute's work.
sector_notes.edu: Finding teachers whose students thrive and learning from them.
sector_notes.com: Communities discovering their own solutions.

key_ideas.defn: People who succeed against the odds, with the same resources as others.
Places where something is already working.
PD's principle that people change by practising, not by being told.
The community leads, discovers and spreads the solution.
A behaviour that explains why a few do better.

pathways.plain_overview: Finding people who already succeed against the odds with the same resources as everyone else, and helping others learn their practices.
pathways.plain_policy: Finding what already works for frontline staff and communities, and spreading it before bringing in outside solutions.

pathways.name: Experiential learning and reflective practice
pathways.overview: Learning as a cycle of doing, noticing, making sense, and trying again. The base layer for learning complexity, because complexity is mostly learned by acting and reflecting.
pathways.road: John Dewey → Kurt Lewin → David Kolb (the experiential learning cycle) → Donald Schön (reflection-in-action)
pathways.mix: Action research, T-groups, improvement cycles
pathways.policy: Learning built into delivery: reflective supervision for frontline staff, learning reviews after each cycle, and training that happens on real cases.

Kurt Lewin: groups, experiential learning, and action research (infed)

pathways.lens: Complexity of practice: real situations do not match the textbook, so learning happens by acting, noticing and adjusting.
explainer: Experiential learning describes learning as a cycle: you have an experience, reflect on it, make sense of it, and try something new. David Kolb's cycle built on John Dewey and Kurt Lewin.

Donald Schön added reflection-in-action: skilled practitioners think while they work, adjusting as surprises come up. Complexity is mostly learned this way, by acting and reflecting, because no rulebook covers it.
practice: After any significant piece of work, write three lines: what happened, what I noticed, what I will try next.
Pair up for reflective supervision once a month.
Notice a surprise during your work and ask what it tells you.
Build learning reviews into the end of each project.

key_ideas.defn: Kolb's cycle: experience, reflection, conceptualization, experimentation.
Schön's idea of thinking on your feet as you work.
Regularly looking back at your work to learn from it.
Argyris and Schön's idea of questioning the assumptions behind your actions, not just the actions.
Dewey's principle that we learn through experience.

pathways.plain_overview: Learning as a cycle of doing, noticing, making sense and trying again: the base layer for learning complexity.
pathways.plain_policy: Learning as part of the job: reflective supervision, a review after each cycle of work, and training on real cases.

pathways.name: Transformative learning
pathways.overview: Learning that changes the frame, not just the content. Often starts with a disorienting dilemma and moves through critical reflection toward a new perspective. Threshold concepts name the ideas that are troublesome before they become obvious.
pathways.road: Jack Mezirow (perspective transformation) → Edward Taylor and Patricia Cranton → Jan Meyer and Ray Land (threshold concepts and troublesome knowledge)

pathways.lens: Complexity of mind: some learning changes the frame through which everything else is seen, and that change is often uncomfortable before it is freeing.
explainer: Transformative learning is learning that changes how you see, not just what you know. Jack Mezirow found that it often starts with a disorienting dilemma, a situation your current assumptions cannot explain, and moves through critical reflection to a new perspective.

Others, like Edward Taylor and Patricia Cranton, broadened the theory. Threshold concepts (Jan Meyer and Ray Land) name the ideas in a field that are troublesome at first but transform understanding once grasped.
practice: Notice a moment when something did not fit your assumptions, and write about what it challenged.
Ask a group what they assumed before a project and what they assume now.
In teaching, identify the threshold concepts learners find troublesome and give them time there.
Make space for discomfort; do not rush to resolve it.

pathways.lens: Complexity as lived and named: people understand the systems around them best when they analyse them from their own experience and act together.
explainer: Critical and popular education treats learning as a practice of freedom. Paulo Freire taught adult literacy in Brazil by starting from learners' own words and lives, so that reading the word became reading the world. He called the awakening of critical awareness conscientization.

Myles Horton's Highlander Folk School trained labour and civil rights leaders, including Rosa Parks. bell hooks wrote about engaged pedagogy that honours students as whole people. The thread: education that helps people name and change the forces shaping their lives.
practice: Start a session with participants' experience of the issue, not with expert input.
Use a code, such as a picture or a story, that people can analyse together.
Ask: why is it this way, who benefits, and what can we do?
Turn learning into action the group chooses.

pathways.lens: Complexity as learning held in groups: knowledge about complex work lives in people's practice, and spreads through relationships over time.
explainer: Communities of practice are groups of people who share a concern or a craft and learn from each other over time. Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger studied how apprentices learn by taking part in such communities.

Action learning, created by Reg Revans, brings small groups together to work on real problems by asking each other questions rather than giving advice. Etienne and Beverly Wenger-Trayner extended these ideas to social learning across whole systems.
practice: Find five to ten people who share your practice and meet monthly.
Bring a real problem to an action learning set and only receive questions for the first half hour.
Keep a shared log of stories and lessons.
Invite newcomers to take part at the edge and grow toward the centre.

pathways.lens: Complexity of mind: the capacity to hold complexity grows over a lifetime, and stuck change often hides a commitment worth understanding.
explainer: Adult development research suggests that adults can keep growing in how they make sense of the world, becoming more able to hold several perspectives, uncertainty and contradiction. Robert Kegan described a series of such shifts in In Over Our Heads.

Kegan and Lisa Lahey's immunity to change explains why people stay stuck: hidden competing commitments protect them from something they fear. Jennifer Garvey Berger made these ideas practical for leaders in complexity. Critics, including Nora Bateson, warn against ranking people by stage.
practice: Map your own immunity to change: goal, what you do instead, hidden worries, big assumptions.
Test one big assumption with a small, safe experiment.
Ask a colleague how they see a problem and try to describe it in their terms.
Avoid using stages to label people; use them to ask what support someone needs.

pathways.lens: Complexity of learning: learning emerges from relationships between learners, teachers and context, and preparing people for an unpredictable world means teaching uncertainty, not only answers.
explainer: This pathway asks what education looks like when we take complexity seriously: classrooms, schools and learning systems are complex systems themselves, and learners face a world no one can predict.

Edgar Morin's Seven Complex Lessons, written for UNESCO, argued that education must teach the human condition, uncertainty and understanding. Brent Davis and Dennis Sumara applied complexity science to teaching. The Inner Development Goals offer a framework of inner capacities for working on global challenges.
practice: Design one lesson around an open question with no single right answer.
Let students explore a local system, like the school's food or energy, as a complex system.
Assess learning by how students handle uncertainty, not only by recall.
Treat the school itself as a learning system: what feedback loops help it improve?
